Leading the pack is **Hamilton**, which continues to set the standard for contemporary musical theater nearly a decade after its debut. Lin-Manuel Rodrigo's hip-hop retelling of American history remains as groundbreaking as ever, earning a 90/100 rating that underscores its enduring impact on the art form.

The season's most pleasant surprise is **Maybe Happy Ending**, a charming robot love story that critics are calling one of Broadway's most original musicals in years. With an 85/100 score, this tender exploration of love and obsolescence proves that fresh ideas still have a home on Broadway. Meanwhile, **Oh, Mary!** offers something completely different—Cole Escola's absurdist farce reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a boozy, cabaret-obsessed narcissist, earning raves for its riotous comedy and fearless irreverence.

The lineup also showcases Broadway's greatest strength: variety. Long-running spectacles like **The Lion King** and **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** deliver visual wonder, while **Hadestown** and the timely **Ragtime** revival demonstrate how classic stories resonate with contemporary audiences. Rounding out the selection are the irreverent satire of **The Book of Mormon**, the infectious rhythms of **Buena Vista Social Club**, and the cynical glamour of **Chicago**.

Whether you're drawn to groundbreaking innovation, laugh-out-loud comedy, or stunning theatrical craft, March 2026 offers something for every theatergoer.

This month's selections demonstrate Broadway's range, from intimate character studies to effects-heavy extravaganzas. Whether you're drawn to sharp-edged comedy, magical spectacle, or franchise expansions, these productions offer distinct theatrical experiences worth exploring.

best-broadway-shows-for-kids.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows for Kids

As of March 2026, Broadway offers a robust selection of family-friendly productions that balance spectacle with storytelling, earning an average critic score of 75 out of 100 across six featured shows.

Leading the pack is **The Lion King**, which continues to set the standard for theatrical innovation nearly three decades after its premiere. Critics consistently praise Julie Taymor's groundbreaking puppetry and costume design, awarding it an 83/100 score across 31 reviews. The production remains a masterclass in visual storytelling that captivates audiences of all ages.

Close behind is **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** (82/100, 69 reviews), which divides critics between its undeniably spectacular stagecraft and a narrative that doesn't always match the magic of its technical achievements. The show's illusions and production values represent some of Broadway's most ambitious work, even as reviewers note unevenness in the story itself.

The remaining selections—**Aladdin**, **& Juliet**, **Wicked**, and **MJ The Musical**—all score between 70-71/100, representing solid if not exceptional options for families. These productions tend to prioritize visual spectacle and recognizable music over narrative complexity, with critics acknowledging their crowd-pleasing appeal while noting formulaic storytelling or sanitized approaches to their subject matter.

What emerges from critical consensus is that today's family theater landscape favors technical wizardry and brand recognition, with established titles dominating the category. Parents should consider whether their children will be more engaged by timeless theatrical artistry, magical special effects, or familiar songs and stories when making their selection.

The show's 83/100 critical average reflects strong consensus around both its artistic execution and cultural timeliness.

On the opposite end of the theatrical spectrum, **Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York)** offers something refreshingly modest: a two-hander rom-com that wins hearts through sincerity rather than spectacle. This British transfer proves that intimate storytelling still has a place among Broadway's grander productions, earning solid reviews for its heartfelt performances.

The revival trend continues with **Chess**, though critics remain split on this ambitious production. While the ABBA score and a powerhouse trio of performers—Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit, and an unnamed Christopher—deliver vocally stunning performances, the show's 65/100 average suggests the production hasn't fully solved the musical's long-standing structural challenges.

With an average critical score of 75/100 across four featured productions, March offers theatergoers quality options ranging from epic musical theater to stripped-down contemporary drama. Whether you're drawn to socially conscious revivals or intimate character studies, this month's Broadway landscape provides entry points for different tastes and sensibilities.

best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows Opening in 2020

As we look back in March 2026 at the Broadway shows that premiered in 2020, we're examining a season dramatically cut short by the pandemic—making the productions that did open all the more significant in theater history.

Leading our rankings is **Les Misérables** (83/100), a grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre that earns critical praise for its fresh approach to the beloved musical, though the reimagining doesn't win over all traditionalists. Close behind, **A Soldier's Play** (78/100) delivers what critics call a powerful and long-overdue Broadway debut for Charles Fuller's Pulitzer-winning drama, with the stellar revival proving the work's examination of race and justice remains urgently relevant.

The season showcases notable literary adaptations and bold reinterpretations. **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100) divides critics between those captivated by Laura Linney's luminous solo performance in this Elizabeth Strout adaptation and those who question the material's theatrical viability. **Grand Horizons** (71/100) offers more traditional fare—a boulevard comedy about late-life divorce that critics find pleasant if familiar, elevated by performances from Jane Alexander and James Cromwell. Rounding out our list, **West Side Story** (68/100) proves the most polarizing entry, with Ivo van Hove's radical reimagining featuring striking video design and visceral staging that either thrills or alienates audiences.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season—brief as it was—demonstrated Broadway's range from classical revivals to daring experimental work. Whether you're drawn to stirring drama, intimate character studies, or bold directorial visions, these productions represent the last complete works before an unprecedented theatrical shutdown.

best-broadway-shows-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2021 represent a remarkable chapter in theater history—productions that reopened the industry after an unprecedented shutdown and redefined what American theater could be.

The class of 2021 demonstrates exceptional range, from intimate experimental works to lavish spectacles. Leading the pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama featuring Deirdre O'Connell's mesmerizing lip-sync performance to a real interview with the playwright's mother. Critics continue to hail it as unforgettable and groundbreaking. Close behind, **The Phantom of the Opera** proves Andrew Lloyd Webber's mega-musical remains irresistible despite—or perhaps because of—its unapologetic camp, while Rebecca Frecknall's **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** earns widespread acclaim for its stunning immersive transformation of the August Wilson Theatre.

The year also brought powerful solo performances, including Ruben Santiago-Hudson's virtuosic **Lackawanna Blues**, and verbatim theater like **Is This a Room**, which transforms an FBI transcript into gripping drama. Epic works like **The Lehman Trilogy** shared stages with Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's urgent **Pass Over**, which made history as Broadway's first show back after the shutdown. Gender-swapped revivals (**Company**), exuberant pop musicals (**SIX**), and warm workplace comedies (**Clyde's**) rounded out a season that proved Broadway could be both commercially viable and artistically daring.

With an average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 season set a high bar for theatrical excellence. Whether you're drawn to experimental boundary-pushing or traditional Broadway spectacle, these shows offer compelling reasons to experience what made this year unforgettable.

best-broadway-shows-2022.intro:

With an average critic score of 83/100 across our top ten shows, this collection represents some of the most celebrated theatrical productions of the decade.

**Kimberly Akimbo** leads our rankings, with critics consistently describing David Lindsay-Abaire and Jeanine Tesori's musical as a near-perfect achievement that masterfully balances quirky humor with profound emotional depth. The show's ability to find comedy and humanity in a story about a teenager with a rare aging condition has resonated deeply with both critics and audiences.

Close behind are two exceptional revivals: a stripped-down **Into the Woods** that serves as a fitting tribute to Stephen Sondheim's legacy, and **A Strange Loop**, Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer-winning meta-musical that critics praise for its brazenly original voice and unflinching honesty.

The 2022 season proves particularly notable for bringing celebrated plays to Broadway audiences, including three Pulitzer winners: Suzan-Lori Parks' **Topdog/Underdog**, Stephen Adly Guirgis's **Between Riverside and Crazy**, and Paula Vogel's **How I Learned to Drive**. Tom Stoppard's deeply personal **Leopoldstadt** rounds out the dramatic offerings with its haunting meditation on Jewish identity and the Holocaust.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting favorites, this collection offers a comprehensive look at a season that delivered both artistic ambition and critical excellence across musicals, dramas, and solo performances.

best-broadway-plays-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of theater just before—and immediately after—an unprecedented global disruption. These productions, which debuted in the brief window before theaters went dark or returned during the industry's cautious reopening, continue to resonate with audiences today.

Leading our selection is **Les Misérables**, which earns an 83/100 from critics for its grittier reimagining at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. This isn't your traditional barricade-storming production; the reboot takes a darker, more visceral approach that has won over most reviewers, even as some purists remain skeptical of the bold new interpretation.

**A Soldier's Play** claims the second spot with a 78/100, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a stellar revival. Critics consistently highlight how this production demonstrates the play's enduring relevance, with its examination of race, power, and identity in the military proving as urgent now as when Fuller first wrote it.

The remaining selections showcase Broadway's range: Laura Linney's tour-de-force solo performance in **My Name is Lucy Barton** divides critics between those enchanted by her luminosity and those who find the adaptation too static, while both **Grand Horizons** and Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining offer contrasting approaches to familiar theatrical territory.

With an average score of 74/100 across these five productions, the class of 2020 reflects a season of artistic ambition and risk-taking. Explore our detailed reviews to discover which of these productions aligns with your theatrical tastes.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2021 represent a remarkable chapter in theater history—the triumphant return of live performance after the pandemic shutdown. These productions, which began reopening stages in the summer and fall of that year, showcase exceptional range: from intimate experimental works to spectacular revivals that redefined classics for new audiences.

Leading our rankings is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama that continues to mesmerize critics with Deirdre O'Connell's stunning lip-sync performance recounting a harrowing true story. Close behind, **The Phantom of the Opera** proves that Lloyd Webber's mega-musical spectacle still captivates despite—or perhaps because of—its unabashed theatricality, while **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** earns widespread acclaim for director Rebecca Frecknall's immersive transformation of the Playhouse Theatre into a visceral Weimar experience.

The 2021 season balances grand-scale productions like **The Lehman Trilogy**'s epic three-hour exploration of American capitalism with intimate solo performances such as **Lackawanna Blues**. Verbatim theater finds powerful expression in **Is This a Room**, while revivals like Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** demonstrate how fresh perspectives can illuminate Sondheim's genius. **Pass Over**, which made history as Broadway's first show back after the shutdown, channels Beckett and Exodus into an urgent examination of Black American experience.

With an impressive average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the class of 2021 set a high bar for theatrical excellence during Broadway's emotional comeback season. Whether you're drawn to experimental docudrama, reimagined classics, or intimate character studies, these shows offer compelling reasons to experience the best of what reopened Broadway stages five years ago.

best-broadway-plays-2022.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the 2022 Broadway season stands out as a remarkable year that brought both innovative new voices and essential revivals to the stage. Four years later, these productions continue to resonate with audiences and shape contemporary theater.

The season's standout is **Kimberly Akimbo**, David Lindsay-Abaire and Jeanine Tesori's musical about a teenager with a rare aging condition. Critics consistently praise its delicate balance of comedy and heartbreak, with 34 reviews averaging an impressive 88/100. The show proves that quirky, character-driven stories can achieve both critical acclaim and commercial success.

Two other productions earned identical 86/100 scores: **Into the Woods**, a stripped-down Sondheim revival that arrived shortly after the composer's death and served as a fitting tribute to his genius, and **A Strange Loop**, Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer Prize-winning meta-musical that broke new ground with its brutally honest exploration of identity and creativity.

The 2022 season also marked a significant moment for Pulitzer Prize-winning works on Broadway. Beyond *A Strange Loop*, the year featured revivals of Suzan-Lori Parks's **Topdog/Underdog**, Paula Vogel's **How I Learned to Drive**, and Stephen Adly Guirgis's **Between Riverside and Crazy**, alongside Tom Stoppard's deeply personal **Leopoldstadt** and Martyna Majok's **Cost of Living**. This concentration of award-winning dramatic literature underscored Broadway's commitment to substantive storytelling.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, the 2022 season demonstrated exceptional quality and range, from Mike Birbiglia's solo show to Jordan E. Cooper's audacious satire **Ain't No Mo'**. Explore these productions to understand a pivotal year in contemporary American theater.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2023 continue to demonstrate the medium's remarkable vitality and range. These productions, now with the benefit of critical distance, have solidified their place in recent theatrical history with an impressive average critic score of 82/100.

The year proves particularly notable for its successful revivals. Maria Friedman's production of **Merrily We Roll Along** leads the pack with an 85/100 score, finally delivering the emotionally resonant staging that eluded Sondheim's notorious 1981 original. **Appropriate**, Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's searing family drama starring Sarah Paulson, earns an 83/100 and widespread recognition as a modern masterpiece of ensemble acting. Meanwhile, **Parade** demonstrates urgent contemporary relevance in its revival, with Ben Platt and Micaela Diamond delivering powerhouse performances that resonate with today's audiences.

The year also showcases theatrical innovation, from the technically stunning **Stranger Things: The First Shadow** (85/100)—a West End transfer that transcends its source material—to **Stereophonic**, an immersive three-hour rock studio drama that critics describe as near-perfect. Comedy and social commentary merge effectively in **Purlie Victorious**, Ossie Davis's 1961 satire that proves bracingly relevant six decades later, and **Fat Ham**, a Pulitzer-winning riff on Hamlet set at a Black family barbecue.

These ten productions represent a cross-section of Broadway's 2023 offerings, from intimate solo performances to large-scale musicals, from bold new works to reimagined classics. For theatergoers and industry observers alike, this collection offers a comprehensive view of what made 2023 a significant year for straight plays on Broadway.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays

As spring 2026 arrives, Broadway audiences continue to enjoy an impressive slate of plays that opened throughout 2025, demonstrating the enduring vitality of both classic American drama and bold new voices.

The season's critical standout is Ivo van Hove's minimalist revival of **All My Sons**, which earns widespread acclaim for transforming Arthur Miller's family tragedy into a powerfully intimate experience. The production's emotional intensity and exceptional ensemble work have made it essential viewing for serious theatergoers. Close behind, the 20th-anniversary revival of **The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee** proves that great musical theater can transcend genre classifications—critics celebrate its airtight writing and surprising emotional depth, finding the show as resonant today as it was two decades ago.

Among newer works, **Liberation**—Bess Wohl's ambitious feminist memory play—stands out for its timeliness and strong performances, even as some critics debate its structural choices. Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer-winning **English** continues to earn praise for its sensitive exploration of language and identity, while Branden Jacobs-Jenkins delivers another characteristically sharp family drama with **Purpose**, blending humor with piercing social observation.

The diversity of offerings extends from David Yazbek's darkly comic **Dead Outlaw**, which chronicles the bizarre afterlife of outlaw Elmer McCurdy, to a timely revival of **Ragtime** anchored by Joshua Henry's powerhouse performance. Even family audiences find sophisticated fare with **Paddington The Musical**, whose remarkably lifelike puppet has become a theatrical marvel in its own right.

With an average critical score of 84/100 across these ten productions, this collection represents Broadway drama firing on all cylinders—offering everything from reimagined classics to urgent new perspectives for discerning audiences seeking substantive theatrical experiences.
